claim: The contrast sensitivity function (CSF) is a fundamental assessment of visual performance that describes how sensitivity varies with the frequency of the stimulus.
source: The contrast sensitivity function (CSF), how sensitivity varies with the frequency of the stimulus, is a fundamental assessment of visual performance.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about the CSF.

claim: The CSF is generally assumed to be determined by low-level sensory processes.
source: The CSF is generally assumed to be determined by low-level sensory processes.
evidence: This represents the prevailing assumption in the field as stated in the abstract.

claim: The spatial sensitivities of neurons in the early visual pathways, as measured in experiments with immobilized eyes, diverge from psychophysical CSF measurements in primates.
source: However, the spatial sensitivities of neurons in the early visual pathways, as measured in experiments with immobilized eyes, diverge from psychophysical CSF measurements in primates.
evidence: This is a key observation stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Humans continually move their eyes even when looking at a fixed point under natural viewing conditions.
source: Under natural viewing conditions, as in typical psychophysical measurements, humans continually move their eyes even when looking at a fixed point.
evidence: This is an established fact about human oculomotor behavior.

claim: The transformation of the spatial scene into temporal modulations on the retina by eye movements reconciles human CSF and the response characteristics of retinal ganglion cells under a broad range of conditions.
source: Here, we show that the resulting transformation of the spatial scene into temporal modulations on the retina constitutes a processing stage that reconciles human CSF and the response characteristics of retinal ganglion cells under a broad range of conditions.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by modeling and data analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Eye movements work synergistically with the spatio-temporal sensitivities of retinal neurons to encode spatial information.
source: Our findings suggest a fundamental integration between perception and action: eye movements work synergistically with the spatio-temporal sensitivities of retinal neurons to encode spatial information.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Contrast sensitivity is one of the most important measures of visual function.
source: Contrast sensitivity, the ability to distinguish a patterned input from a uniform background, is one of the most important measures of visual function (Robson, 1966; Campbell and Robson, 1968; De Valois et al., 1974; Owsley and sensitivity, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to foundational work in the field.

claim: Under photopic conditions, the CSF measured with stationary gratings exhibits a band-pass shape that typically peaks around 3–5 cycles/deg and sharply declines at higher and lower spatial frequencies.
source: Under photopic conditions, the CSF measured with stationary gratings exhibits a well-known band-pass shape that typically peaks around 3–5 cycles/deg and sharply declines at higher and lower spatial frequencies.
evidence: This is an established characteristic of the CSF based on prior research.

claim: At high frequency, a decline in sensitivity is expected due to the filtering of the eyes' optics and the spatial limits in sampling imposed by the cone mosaic on the retina.
source: At high frequency, a decline in sensitivity is expected for several reasons, including the filtering of the eyes' optics (Campbell and Green, 1965) and the spatial limits in sampling imposed by the cone mosaic on the retina (Hirsch and Miller, 1987; Rossi and Roorda, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on optical filtering and photoreceptor sampling.

claim: The reasons for reduced sensitivity at low spatial frequencies have remained less clear.
source: At low frequencies, however, the reasons for a reduced sensitivity have remained less clear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in understanding that the study addresses.

claim: A popular theory links the low-frequency attenuation in visual sensitivity to the neural mechanisms of early visual encoding.
source: A popular theory directly links the low-frequency attenuation in visual sensitivity to the neural mechanisms of early visual encoding (Atick and Redlich, 1990; Atick and Redlich, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Atick and Redlich's work on efficient coding.

claim: Retinal ganglion cells respond less strongly at low spatial frequencies to counterbalance the spectral distribution of natural scenes, according to efficient coding theory.
source: Building on theories of efficient coding (Barlow, 1961), it has been argued that this attenuation reflects a form of matching between the characteristics of the natural visual world and the response tuning of neurons in the retina: retinal ganglion cells (henceforth RGCs) respond less strongly at low spatial frequencies so as to counterbalance the spectral distribution of natural scenes.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal cited from prior work.

claim: The efficient coding proposal conflicts with experimental data showing that the spatial frequency response of retinal ganglion cells deviates sharply from the CSF.
source: Although very influential, this proposal conflicts with experimental data. Neurophysiological recordings have long shown that the way the responses of retinal ganglion cells vary with spatial frequency deviates sharply from the CSF.
evidence: This is a key observation that motivates the study, based on prior neurophysiological data.

claim: The CSF of macaques is very similar to that of humans.
source: The CSF of macaques is very similar to that of humans (De Valois et al., 1974)
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Valois et al. 1974.

claim: Neurons in the macaque retina respond much more strongly at low spatial frequencies than expected from behavioral measurements of the CSF.
source: yet neurons in the macaque retina respond much more strongly at low spatial frequencies than one would expect from behavioral measurements of the CSF (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1A comparing neuronal and behavioral measurements.

claim: The deviation between neuronal responses and the CSF persists even when accounting for differences in stimuli and nonlinear attenuation in responsiveness at low spatial frequencies.
source: This deviation cannot be reconciled with standard models of retinal ganglion cells. It persists even when one takes into account obvious differences in the stimuli often used in neurophysiological and behavioral measurements (i.e. drifting gratings vs. temporally modulated gratings), as well as the nonlinear attenuation in responsiveness at low spatial frequencies exhibited by some retinal ganglion cells (Derrington and Lennie, 1984; Croner and Kaplan, 1995; Benardete and Kaplan, 1997a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple neurophysiological studies.

claim: The mismatch between neuronal and behavioral sensitivity indicates that additional mechanisms contribute to the CSF.
source: This mismatch between neuronal and behavioral sensitivity indicates that additional mechanisms contribute to the CSF.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observed mismatch.

claim: Fixational eye movements include small saccades (microsaccades) and fixational drift.
source: Fixational eye movements (FEMs; red curve in magnified inset and black and gray traces in Cartesian graph), which include small saccades (microsaccades; red-shaded interval) and fixational drift (green), continually displace the stimulus on the retina.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the caption.

claim: Fixational eye movements continually displace the stimulus on the retina.
source: Fixational eye movements (FEMs; red curve in magnified inset and black and gray traces in Cartesian graph), which include small saccades (microsaccades; red-shaded interval) and fixational drift (green), continually displace the stimulus on the retina.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Eye drift profoundly reshapes visual input signals by redistributing the 0 Hz (DC) power of the external static stimulus to non-zero temporal frequencies on the retina.
source: In previous work, we have shown that eye drift profoundly reshapes visual input signals, redistributing the 0 Hz (DC) power of the external static stimulus to non-zero temporal frequencies on the retina (Casile and Rucci, 2006; Casile and Rucci, 2009; Kuang et al., 2012; Aytekin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Oculomotor-induced luminance fluctuations appear to be used by humans for fine spatial discrimination.
source: These modulations appear to be used by humans for the fine spatial discrimination (Rucci et al., 2007; Boi et al., 2017; Ratnam et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Contrast sensitivity is affected by temporal modulations in the stimulus.
source: In addition to the properties described above, it is well established that contrast sensitivity is affected by temporal modulations in the stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact.

claim: The shape of the CSF changes from band-pass to low-pass as the temporal frequency of the stimulus increases.
source: Although the CSF exhibits a strong attenuation at low spatial frequencies when tested with stationary gratings, the shape of this function changes when gratings are modulated in time, transitioning from band-pass to low-pass as the temporal frequency of the stimulus increases (Robson, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robson 1966.

claim: Sensitivity tends to shift to higher spatial frequencies when retinal image motion is strongly reduced in experiments of retinal stabilization.
source: Furthermore, although strongly attenuated, sensitivity also tends to shift to higher spatial frequencies when retinal image motion is strongly reduced, as in experiments of retinal stabilization (Kelly, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kelly 1979.

claim: The mean receptive fields of ganglion cells in the primate retina deviate considerably from the contrast sensitivity of alert and behaving macaques, especially at low spatial frequencies.
source: Figure 1A compares the mean receptive fields of ganglion cells in the primate retina, as estimated by Croner and Kaplan (1995), with the contrast sensitivity of alert and behaving macaques (De Valois et al., 1974). The two sets of data deviate considerably, especially at low spatial frequencies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by citations.

claim: Neural sensitivity at low spatial frequencies is not strongly attenuated, unlike the CSF, a trend reported by multiple neurophysiological studies.
source: In this range, unlike the CSF, neural sensitivity is not strongly attenuated, a trend reported by multiple neurophysiological studies (e.g., Kaplan and Shapley, 1982; Hicks et al., 1983; Derrington and Lennie, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple neurophysiological studies.

claim: Neural responses have been directly measured at very low spatial frequencies (down to 0.07 cpd).
source: This deviation is not simply the outcome of incorrectly extrapolating receptive-field measurements, as neural responses have been directly measured at very low spatial frequencies (down to 0.07 cpd in Croner and Kaplan, 1995; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Croner and Kaplan 1995 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: A difference-of-Gaussians model can yield reduced responses at low spatial frequencies, but attenuation similar to the CSF requires highly unrealistic model parameters.
source: While a difference-of-Gaussians model can yield reduced responses at low spatial frequencies, attenuation similar to that observed in the CSF can only be achieved at the expense of highly unrealistic model parameters.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For both M and P cells, matching the physiological CSF requires a surround strength that is more than twice the value found in physiological measurements.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B, for both M and P cells, matching the physiological CSF requires a surround strength that is more than twice the value found in physiological measurements, a condition that gives an almost perfect balance between excitation and inhibition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Even small deviations from the balance between excitation and inhibition lead to marked departures from the CSF.
source: Even small deviations from this balance lead to marked departures from the CSF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: The spatial sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells appears to be quantitatively incompatible with the characteristics of the CSF.
source: Thus, contrary to previous proposals, the spatial sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells appears to be quantitatively incompatible with the characteristics of the CSF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of difference-of-Gaussians models.

claim: A greater attenuation of neural sensitivity is required at low spatial frequencies to counterbalance the large power of natural scenes in this range.
source: A greater attenuation of neural sensitivity is required at low spatial frequencies to counterbalance the large power of natural scenes in this range.
evidence: This is an inference from the mismatch between neuronal responses and the CSF.

claim: Experimenters often take great care to minimize temporal transients by slowly ramping up the stimulus at the beginning and down at the end of a trial and by enforcing fixation to prevent visual changes caused by saccadic eye movements.
source: Experimenters often take great care to minimize these transients, for example by slowly ramping up the stimulus at the beginning and down at the end of a trial and by enforcing fixation to prevent visual changes caused by saccadic eye movements (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes standard experimental procedures, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Despite precautions, fixational eye movements are always present and modulate the visual flow impinging on the retina even when the stimulus does not change on the monitor.
source: Yet, despite these precautions, fixational eye movements are always present and modulate the visual flow impinging on the retina even when the stimulus does not change on the monitor.
evidence: This is an established fact about fixational eye movements.

claim: The same amount of fixational drift yields larger temporal fluctuations with gratings at higher spatial frequencies.
source: Fixational jitter modulates input signals in a way that depends on the spatial frequency of the stimulus. The same amount of fixational drift yields larger temporal fluctuations with gratings at higher spatial frequencies (vertical arrows).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Higher spatial frequencies lead to broader temporal distributions of input power.
source: Input power with gratings at 1 and 8 cycles/deg (left panel). Higher spatial frequencies lead to broader temporal distributions (right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Because of the characteristics of ocular drift, the resulting dynamic power increases with spatial frequency, up to approximately 30 cpd.
source: As shown in Figure 2C–D, because of the characteristics of ocular drift, the resulting dynamic power increases with spatial frequency, up to approximately 30 cpd (magenta line in Figure 2D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C–D.

claim: 30 cpd roughly corresponds to the frequency limit given by the spatial resolution of photoreceptors in the fovea.
source: which, interestingly, roughly corresponds to the frequency limit given by the spatial resolution of photoreceptors in the fovea.
evidence: This is an observation connecting the data to known anatomical constraints.

claim: Contrast modulations due to the onset/offset of the stimulus on the display cause power redistributions that do not depend on the spatial frequency of the stimulus.
source: In contrast, unlike drift, contrast modulations due to the onset/offset of the stimulus on the display cause power redistributions that do not depend on the spatial frequency of the stimulus (black line in Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Eye movements do not generate new power in the retinal input; they only redistribute the original DC power of the stimulus.
source: It is important to keep in mind that eye movements do not generate new power in the retinal input. They only redistribute the original DC power of the stimulus, so that a complementary frequency-dependent attenuation of power occurs along the 0 Hz axis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a theoretical point illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both eye drift and contrast changes yield temporal modulations that are well within the range of temporal sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells.
source: Both eye drift and contrast changes yield temporal modulations that are well within the range of temporal sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells (cfg. Figure 2C and E).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 2C and E.

claim: In simulations that replicated the standard conditions of contrast sensitivity measurements, drift modulations predominated.
source: However, in simulations that replicated the standard conditions of contrast sensitivity measurements, drift modulations predominated.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations performed in the study.

claim: Since drift modulations convey little power at low spatial frequencies, the responses of standard ganglion cells were attenuated in this frequency range.
source: Since drift modulations convey little power at low spatial frequencies, the responses of standard ganglion cells were attenuated in this frequency range (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B–C.

claim: A simple linear combination of the resulting M and P responses accurately predicted human contrast sensitivity with stationary stimuli over the entire range of relevant spatial frequencies.
source: As a consequence of this effect, a simple linear combination of the resulting M and P responses accurately predicted human contrast sensitivity with stationary stimuli over the entire range of relevant spatial frequencies (solid line in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the absence of eye movements, when the only temporal modulations were those given by the onset/offset of the stimulus on the monitor, the CSF predicted by the same linear combination of neural responses exhibited a low-pass behavior that deviated considerably from human contrast sensitivity.
source: In contrast, in the absence of eye movements, when the only temporal modulations were those given by the onset/offset of the stimulus on the monitor, the CSF predicted by the same linear combination of neural responses exhibited a low-pass behavior that deviated considerably from human contrast sensitivity, especially at low spatial frequencies (dashed lines in Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: No linear combination of modeled responses could approximate the CSF in the absence of eye movements.
source: In fact, no linear combination of modeled responses could approximate the CSF in this condition.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: Without taking ocular drift into account, neuronal models exhibit a higher level of response at low spatial frequencies, which strongly deviates from the CSF.
source: Thus, without taking ocular drift into account, neuronal models exhibit a higher level of response at low spatial frequencies, as dictated by the spatial sensitivity of their kernels — and this strongly deviates from the CSF (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is a key finding of the study.

claim: Standard models of the responses of M and P RGCs well predict the shape of the human CSF as measured with stationary gratings, but only when one considers sensitivity to the temporal modulations caused on the retina by fixational drift.
source: In sum, standard models of the responses of M and P RGCs well predict the shape of the human CSF as measured with stationary gratings, but only when one considers sensitivity to the temporal modulations caused on the retina by fixational drift.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: The CSF in humans is not space-time separable: the way contrast sensitivity varies with spatial frequency depends on the temporal frequency of the modulation.
source: Measurements with gratings modulated in time have long shown that the CSF in humans is not space-time separable: the way contrast sensitivity varies with spatial frequency depends on the temporal frequency of the modulation (Robson, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robson 1966.

claim: The same linear combination of the responses of M and P cells as in Figure 3 continued to closely match human performance when the stimulus was temporally modulated on the display.
source: The same linear combination of the responses of M and P cells as in Figure 3 continued to closely match human performance when the stimulus was temporally modulated on the display, and the predicted CSF replicated the low-pass to band-pass transition observed in primates, as the frequency of the modulation increased (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The predicted CSF replicated the low-pass to band-pass transition observed in primates as the frequency of the modulation increased.
source: The same linear combination of the responses of M and P cells as in Figure 3 continued to closely match human performance when the stimulus was temporally modulated on the display, and the predicted CSF replicated the low-pass to band-pass transition observed in primates, as the frequency of the modulation increased (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The change in CSF shape was the consequence of the different amount of dynamic power that the combination of fixational drift and temporal modulations of the stimulus delivered within the range of neuronal sensitivity.
source: This change in shape was the consequence of the different amount of dynamic power that the combination of fixational drift and temporal modulations of the stimulus delivered within the range of neuronal sensitivity.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed change in CSF shape.

claim: Flickering a grating has the effect of shifting the 0 Hz power of the grating to the temporal frequency of the modulation.
source: However, flickering a grating has the effect of shifting the 0 Hz power of the grating to the temporal frequency of the modulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: At low temporal modulating frequencies (e.g. 1 Hz or below), only a small fraction of DC power was within the region of neuronal sensitivity, and the temporal redistribution resulting from eye drift continued to exert a strong influence, forcing the CSF to maintain its band-pass shape.
source: At low temporal modulating frequencies (e.g. 1 Hz or below), only a small fraction of this power was within the region of neuronal sensitivity, and the temporal redistribution resulting from eye drift continued to exert a strong influence, forcing the CSF to maintain its band-pass shape.
evidence: This is an explanation for the maintenance of band-pass shape at low temporal frequencies.

claim: At higher temporal frequencies (e.g. 6 Hz and higher), the power restricted to the 0 Hz axis in the absence of stimulus' modulations became fully available within the cells' peak sensitivity region.
source: However, at higher temporal frequencies (e.g. 6 Hz and higher), the power restricted to the 0 Hz axis in the absence of stimulus' modulations now became fully available within the cells' peak sensitivity region.
evidence: This is an explanation for the transition to low-pass behavior at higher temporal frequencies.

claim: Static power is predominantly at low spatial frequencies.
source: Since this static power is predominantly at low spatial frequencies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), it caused a transition from band-pass to low-pass behavior in the responses of simulated M and P neurons, as well as in the shape of the CSF.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Estimates of the CSF at intermediate frequencies between 0 Hz and 6 Hz suggest that the band-pass to low-pass transition occurs around 3 Hz.
source: Estimates of the CSF at intermediate frequencies between 0 Hz and 6 Hz (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) suggest that this transition occurs around 3 Hz, which is in agreement with psychophysical results (Bowker and Tulunay-Keesey, 1983).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and supported by citation to Bowker and Tulunay-Keesey 1983.

claim: The model attributes the space-time inseparability of the CSF to the structure of the temporal modulations delivered within the range of sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells.
source: In sum, our model attributes the space-time inseparability of the CSF to the structure of the temporal modulations delivered within the range of sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Modulations resulting from eye drift yield a band-pass CSF, whereas sinusoidally modulated gratings yield a low-pass CSF.
source: Modulations resulting from eye drift yield a band-pass CSF, whereas sinusoidally modulated gratings yield a low-pass CSF.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's predictions.

claim: The interplay between eye drift and stimulus modulations explains not only contrast sensitivity with stationary gratings, but also the band-pass to low-pass transition that occurs with temporally modulated gratings.
source: The interplay between these two components of the retinal input explains not only contrast sensitivity with stationary gratings, but also the band-pass to low-pass transition that occurs with temporally modulated gratings.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's explanatory power.

claim: The model correctly predicts the temporal frequency range at which the band-pass to low-pass transition takes place.
source: Notably, it correctly predicts the temporal frequency range at which this transition takes place.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's predictive accuracy.

claim: The results suggest a functional link between the physiological instability of visual fixation and the characteristics of the CSF.
source: Our results, thus, suggest a functional link between the physiological instability of visual fixation and the characteristics of the CSF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: In the complete absence of eye movements, neural responses in the model would only be driven by the modulations present in the external stimulus.
source: Ideally, in the complete absence of eye movements, neural responses in our model would only be driven by the modulations present in the external stimulus.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Under conditions of complete absence of eye movements, the model predicts that sensitivity to a stationary grating would be greatly attenuated and the CSF would shift toward a low-pass shape.
source: Under such conditions, the model predicts that sensitivity to a stationary grating would be greatly attenuated and the CSF would shift toward a low-pass shape, as it would lack the frequency-dependent amplification operated by ocular drift.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Retinal stabilization is always affected by noise in the oculomotor recordings as well as imperfections in gaze-contingent display control, which leave some residual motion on the retina.
source: In real experiments, however, elimination of oculomotor-induced luminance modulations is impossible. Retinal stabilization — a laboratory procedure that attempts to immobilize an image on the retina (Riggs et al., 1953; Yarbus, 1957) — is always affected by noise in the oculomotor recordings as well as imperfections in gaze-contingent display control, which leave some residual motion on the retina.
evidence: This is a description of the limitations of retinal stabilization experiments, supported by citations.

claim: Under retinal stabilization conditions, contrast sensitivity has been found to be attenuated, but it maintains its band-pass shape and peaks at higher spatial frequencies.
source: Under these conditions, contrast sensitivity has indeed been found to be attenuated, but it maintains its band-pass shape and peaks at higher spatial frequencies (Kelly, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kelly 1979.

claim: A Brownian model well captures the characteristics of retinal image motion during fixation.
source: Previous studies have established that a Brownian model well captures the characteristics of retinal image motion during fixation (Kuang et al., 2012; Poletti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reducing the scale of retinal image motion is functionally equivalent to spatially stretching the stimulus.
source: This happens because reducing the scale of retinal image motion is functionally equivalent to spatially stretching the stimulus, which translates, in the Fourier domain, to a compression of the axis of spatial frequencies that moves the amplification range toward higher spatial frequencies.
evidence: This is an explanation for the shift in amplification range.

claim: Model predictions closely followed psychophysical measurements when the diffusion constant of the retinal image motion was attenuated by a factor of 125: a reduction in the amount of retinal image motion attenuated contrast sensitivity while maintaining its band-pass shape and shifted its peak sensitivity to higher spatial frequencies from 4 Hz to 5.5 Hz.
source: Figure 5B compares classical retinal stabilization data from Kelly (1979) to the sensitivity predicted by our model when the diffusion constant of the retinal image motion was attenuated by a factor of 125, which corresponds to shrinking the spatial scale of eye movements by approximately one order of magnitude. Model predictions closely followed psychophysical measurements: a reduction in the amount of retinal image motion attenuated contrast sensitivity while maintaining its band-pass shape and shifted its peak sensitivity to higher spatial frequencies from 4 Hz to 5.5 Hz (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and compared to data from Kelly 1979.

claim: Consideration of the luminance modulations resulting from the motion of the stimulus on the retina accounts for behavioral sensitivity measurements performed in the presence of normal eye movements and under conditions of retinal stabilization.
source: These data show that consideration of the luminance modulations resulting from the motion of the stimulus on the retina accounts not only for behavioral sensitivity measurements performed in the presence of normal eye movements, but also for measurements made under conditions of retinal stabilization, when retinal image motion is greatly reduced.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analysis.

claim: A temporal scheme of spatial encoding predicts the dependencies of contrast sensitivity on spatial and temporal frequency when the temporal modulations introduced by incessant eye movements are taken into account.
source: Here, we show that a temporal scheme of spatial encoding, a scheme in which spatial vision is driven by temporal changes, predicts such dependencies when the temporal modulations introduced by incessant eye movements are taken into account.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: When the consequences of fixational drift are ignored, the known response characteristics of retinal ganglion cells fail to account for human CSF.
source: In contrast, when these consequences of fixational drift are ignored, the known response characteristics of retinal ganglion cells fail to account for human CSF.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: Existing theories of visual processing have attributed the shape of the CSF to the characteristics of early visual processing.
source: An important consequence of our results regards the strategies by which the visual system encodes spatial information. Existing theories of visual processing have attributed the shape of the CSF to the characteristics of early visual processing.
evidence: This describes existing theories in the field.

claim: Atick and Redlich found that the theoretical filter that optimally decorrelates natural images closely matches the CSF.
source: In an influential study (Atick and Redlich, 1992) found that the theoretical filter that optimally decorrelates natural images closely matches the CSF.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Atick and Redlich 1992.

claim: Atick and Redlich assumed that the CSF reflects the average spatial selectivity of ganglion cells in the retina.
source: Since decorrelated responses enable compact neural representations, these authors assumed that the CSF reflects the average spatial selectivity of ganglion cells in the retina.
evidence: This describes the assumption made by Atick and Redlich.

claim: Broad spatial correlations in RGCs responses have been found in preparations in which natural images are displayed in the absence of eye movements.
source: As expected from this deviation, broad spatial correlations in RGCs responses have been found in preparations in which natural images are displayed in the absence of eye movements (Puchalla et al., 2005; Segal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Puchalla et al. 2005 and Segal et al. 2015.

claim: When the transients in stimulus presentation override the consequences of eye drift, spatial sensitivity follows the spatial kernels of modeled receptive fields.
source: These findings are consistent with our model: when the transients in stimulus presentation override the consequences of eye drift, spatial sensitivity follows the spatial kernels of modeled receptive fields.
evidence: This is an explanation consistent with the model.

claim: Responses to low spatial frequencies are enhanced relative to the level that would be needed for decorrelating activity when stimulus transients override eye drift effects.
source: For this reason, responses to low spatial frequencies are enhanced relative to the level that would be needed for decorrelating activity.
evidence: This is a consequence of the model's explanation.

claim: The CSF is shaped by the joint spatial and temporal characteristics of retinal responses and how they interact with oculomotor transients.
source: Rather than attributing spatial sensitivity solely to the spatial selectivity of RGCs, our analysis shows that the CSF is shaped by the joint spatial and temporal characteristics of retinal responses and how they interact with oculomotor transients.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claim: The model predicts the complex way contrast sensitivity varies with the spatial and temporal frequency of the stimulus by a linear combination of the space-time separable functions of P and M channels.
source: It predicts the complex way contrast sensitivity varies with the spatial and temporal frequency of the stimulus by a linear combination of the space-time separable functions of P and M channels.
evidence: This describes the model's predictive capability.

claim: The study cannot exclude that other mechanisms, at various stages of visual processing, may also play a role in shaping the CSF.
source: While our study cannot exclude that other mechanisms, at various stages of visual processing, may also play a role in shaping the CSF (e.g. the number of neurons in different frequency channels), it suggests that these other contributions are minimal.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations of the study.

claim: Consideration of RGCs temporal sensitivity provides a parsimonious unifying framework for a wide range of experimental measurements of the CSF with only a minimal set of assumptions.
source: Consideration of RGCs temporal sensitivity provides a parsimonious unifying framework for a wide range of experimental measurements of the CSF with only a minimal set of assumptions.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: The model assumed that retinal ganglion cells possess negligible sensitivity below the frequencies at which sensitivity can practically be measured (~0.2–0.3 Hz).
source: In our model, we assumed that retinal ganglion cells possess negligible sensitivity below the frequencies at which sensitivity can practically be measured (~0.2–0.3 Hz).
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the model.

claim: Measuring sensitivity in the low temporal frequency range is challenging because it requires trials with long durations, consideration of the visual stimuli present before and after each trial, and estimation of long impulse responses.
source: However, in both neurophysiological and psychophysical experiments, measuring sensitivity in this range is challenging because it requires trials with long durations, consideration of the visual stimuli present before and after each trial, and estimation of long impulse responses.
evidence: This describes experimental challenges.

claim: The few studies that specifically examined retinal ganglion cells' responses at low temporal frequencies found a decline in sensitivity up to the limit that they could measure.
source: The few studies that specifically examined retinal ganglion cells' responses at low temporal frequencies found a decline in sensitivity up to the limit that they could measure (Victor, 1987; Purpura et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Victor 1987 and Purpura et al. 1990.

claim: The response attenuation at low temporal frequencies takes the form of an approximately linear decrease in log-log scale.
source: These studies suggest that the response attenuation takes the form of an approximately linear decrease in log-log scale.
evidence: This is based on prior studies.

claim: Temporal signals at frequencies below ~0.3 Hz are not likely to be useful to an observer in a psychophysical experiment, as they will contain noise power due to visual stimulation on previous trials and during the intertrial interval.
source: Furthermore, temporal signals at frequencies below ~0.3 Hz, even if present, are not likely to be useful to an observer in a psychophysical experiment, as they will contain noise power due to visual stimulation on previous trials and during the intertrial interval (such as eye-blinks and glances around the lab).
evidence: This is a reasoning about the practical utility of low-frequency signals.

claim: The results are robust to the specifics of how low-frequency attenuation in sensitivity was implemented.
source: Our results are robust to the specifics of how this low-frequency attenuation in sensitivity was implemented.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The study specifically focused on fixational drift because of its ubiquitous presence and its known influence on fine pattern vision.
source: We specifically focused on fixational drift both because of its ubiquitous presence and its known influence on fine pattern vision (Ratliff and Riggs, 1950; Ditchburn, 1955; Steinman et al., 1973; Rucci et al., 2007; Ratnam et al., 2017).
evidence: This explains the focus of the study, supported by citations.

claim: Saccades and microsaccades tend to be suppressed during measurements of contrast sensitivity and were not considered in this study.
source: Other types of eye movements, like saccades and microsaccades, tend to be suppressed during measurements of contrast sensitivity (Mostofi et al., 2016) and were not considered in this study.
evidence: This describes the scope of the study, supported by citation.

claim: The transients from saccades and microsaccades differ in their spectra from those from eye drift, as they provide equal temporal power across a broad range of spatial frequencies.
source: The transients from these movements, however, differ in their spectra from those from eye drift, as they provide equal temporal power across a broad range of spatial frequencies.
evidence: This is a characterization of the spectral properties of different eye movements.

claim: During normal viewing, the visual system could benefit from different types of modulations from different eye movements.
source: Thus, during normal viewing, the visual system could benefit from different types of modulations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of different eye movements.

claim: The stereotypical alternation of oculomotor transients resulting from the natural saccade/drift cycle contributes to a coarse-to-fine processing dynamics at each visual fixation.
source: In keeping with this idea, it has been argued that the stereotypical alternation of oculomotor transients resulting from the natural saccade/drift cycle contributes to a coarse-to-fine processing dynamics at each visual fixation (Boi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boi et al. 2017.

claim: The results are very robust and do not depend on fitting model parameters.
source: It is worth emphasizing that our results are very robust and do not depend on fitting model parameters.
evidence: This emphasizes the robustness of the findings.

claim: The study used real traces recorded from human subjects during measurements of contrast sensitivity rather than modeling eye movements.
source: With regard to oculomotor activity, we did not model eye movements, but used real traces recorded from human subjects during measurements of contrast sensitivity.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The study implemented standard M and P filters obtained from the neurophysiological literature and frequently adopted by modeling studies.
source: With regard to neuronal properties, we implemented standard M and P filters obtained from the neurophysiological literature and frequently adopted by modeling studies (Croner and Kaplan, 1995; Benardete and Kaplan, 1997a; Benardete and Kaplan, 1999).
evidence: This describes the methodology, supported by citations.

claim: The two parameters (global gain and M-P ratio) were merely used to quantitatively align the modeled CSF with the experimental data and have no role in explaining the shape of the CSF and its band- to low-pass transition.
source: Our two parameters (the global gain at a given temporal frequency and the ratio of M-P contributions, see Equation 7 in the Materials and methods section) were merely used to quantitatively align the modeled CSF with the experimental data. They have no role in explaining the shape of the CSF and its band- to low-pass transition.
evidence: This clarifies the role of model parameters.

claim: The results predict that the response selectivity of RGCs will change when measured in the presence and absence of the fixational motion of the retinal image.
source: At the neural level, our results predict that the response selectivity of RGCs will change when measured in the presence and absence of the fixational motion of the retinal image.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Neurophysiological studies suggest that fixational eye movements are an important component of visual encoding.
source: Neurophysiological studies already suggest that fixational eye movements are an important component of visual encoding (Gur et al., 1997; Leopold and Logothetis, 1998; Martinez-Conde et al., 2000; Olveczky et al., 2003; Kagan et al., 2008; Meirovithz et al., 2012; McFarland et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Eye jitter has been found to reduce redundancy in the responses of retinal neurons.
source: Eye jitter has been found to reduce redundancy in the responses of retinal neurons (Segal et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Segal et al. 2015.

claim: Eye jitter has been found to synchronize retinal neurons, enhancing visual features.
source: and to synchronize them, enhancing visual features (Greschner et al., 2002) even beyond the physiological limitations imposed by photoreceptors spacing (Juusola et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Greschner et al. 2002 and Juusola et al. 2016.

claim: Retinal ganglion cells have been found that may distinguish between the global motion given by fixational eye movements and the local motion of objects.
source: Furthermore, retinal ganglion cells have been found that may distinguish between the global motion given by fixational eye movements and the local motion of objects (Olveczky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olveczky et al. 2003.

claim: Retinal responses are traditionally measured with the eyes immobilized, a condition in which RGCs tend to exhibit relatively strong responses at low spatial frequencies.
source: Yet, retinal responses are traditionally measured with the eyes immobilized, a condition in which RGCs tend to exhibit relatively strong responses at low spatial frequencies (Croner and Kaplan, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Croner and Kaplan 1995.

claim: The model predicts that the spatial frequency amplification produced by fixational drift in the retinal input will enhance neuronal sensitivity to higher spatial frequencies and will reduce sensitivity to low spatial frequencies.
source: Our model predicts that the spatial frequency amplification produced by fixational drift in the retinal input (Figure 2D) will enhance neuronal sensitivity to higher spatial frequencies and will reduce sensitivity to low spatial frequencies.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model, referencing Figure 2D.

claim: The model predicts that RGCs' spatial sensitivity should exhibit a more pronounced band-pass behavior and its peak should shift toward higher frequencies when measured in the presence of fixational drift.
source: As a consequence, RGCs' spatial sensitivity should exhibit a more pronounced band-pass behavior and its peak should shift toward higher frequencies.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The prediction about RGCs' spatial sensitivity is difficult to test in vivo because of the need to completely stabilize the retinal input, but it can be thoroughly investigated in vitro where the motion of the retinal image is under full experimental control.
source: This prediction is difficult to test in vivo, because of the need to completely stabilize the retinal input, but it can be thoroughly investigated in vitro, where the motion of the retinal image is under full experimental control.
evidence: This discusses the testability of the prediction.

claim: The amplitude of fixational instability regulates the power available in different spatial frequency bands.
source: At the perceptual level, an interesting observation comes from the changes in the frequency content of the retinal input shown in Figure 5A. The amplitude of fixational instability regulates the power available in different spatial frequency bands.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The smaller the amount of retinal image motion, the more the range of amplification shifts to higher spatial frequencies.
source: Specifically, the smaller the amount of retinal image motion, the more the range of amplification shifts to higher spatial frequencies.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis.

claim: The visual system could exploit the relationship between drift amplitude and spatial frequency content by dynamically matching the spatial scale of eye drift to the frequency content of the visual scene or the frequency range that is task-relevant.
source: The visual system could, in principle, exploit this relationship by dynamically matching the spatial scale of eye drift to the frequency content of the visual scene, or the frequency range that is task-relevant.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential visual system strategies.

claim: Within a certain range, smaller drifts would optimize information accrual when foveating on regions rich in high spatial frequencies.
source: Within a certain range, smaller drifts would optimize information accrual when foveating on regions rich in high spatial frequencies.
evidence: This is a speculation about optimal oculomotor strategies.

claim: Several studies support the idea that humans can control the amount of their ocular drift.
source: Indeed, several studies support the idea that humans can control the amount of their ocular drift (Steinman et al., 1973; Cherici et al., 2012; Poletti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The relationship between fixational drift and the frequency content of the retinal input may explain individual perceptual differences.
source: In the same vein, the relationship between fixational drift and the frequency content of the retinal input may also explain individual perceptual differences.
evidence: This is a speculation about sources of individual differences.

claim: Subjects with relatively smaller drifts are expected to perform better in tasks in which high spatial frequencies are critical.
source: Subjects with relatively smaller drifts are expected to perform better in tasks in which high spatial frequencies are critical.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The model predicts that manipulating temporal modulations from eye drift will affect performance.
source: Furthermore, our model predicts that manipulating temporal modulations from eye drift will affect performance.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Enlarging fixational jitter increases the amount of power available at low spatial frequencies predicting an improvement in contrast sensitivity in this range.
source: In the other direction, enlarging fixational jitter increases the amount of power available at low spatial frequencies predicting an improvement in contrast sensitivity in this range.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The prediction about enlarging fixational jitter is consistent with the improvements in word and object recognition reported in patients with central visual loss when images or text are jittered or scrolled.
source: This prediction is consistent with the improvements in word and object recognition reported in patients with central visual loss, when images or text are jittered or scrolled (Watson et al., 2012; Harvey and Walker, 2014; Gustafsson and Inde, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on patients with central visual loss.

claim: The spatial frequency band of retinal ganglion cells decreases with eccentricity.
source: The spatial frequency band of retinal ganglion cells decreases with eccentricity
evidence: This is an established fact about retinal organization.

claim: Enlarging retinal image motion has the effect of bringing more power in the range of sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells at higher eccentricities.
source: and enlarging retinal image motion has the effect of bringing more power in their range of sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference about the effects of image motion at different eccentricities.

claim: The study predicts that disturbances in fixational oculomotor control will affect visual sensitivity.
source: Our study also has clinical implications, as it predicts that disturbances in fixational oculomotor control will affect visual sensitivity.
evidence: This is a prediction with clinical implications.

claim: Oculomotor anomalies and impaired sensitivity co-occur in a variety of disorders, including dyslexia and schizophrenia.
source: Oculomotor anomalies and impaired sensitivity co-occur in a variety of disorders, including conditions as diverse as dyslexia (Stein and Fowler, 1981; Stein and Fowler, 1993) and schizophrenia (Dowiasch et al., 2016; Egaña et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on dyslexia and schizophrenia.

claim: Patients with dyslexia and schizophrenia exhibit similar visual deficits including reduced sensitivity, low-level visual impairments, and reading disabilities.
source: Patients with these conditions exhibit similar visual deficits including reduced sensitivity (Lovegrove et al., 1980a; Lovegrove et al., 1980b; Slaghuis, 1998), low-level visual impairments (Eden et al., 1996; Li, 2002; Butler et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2006) and reading disabilities (Revheim et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Reading disabilities in dyslexia and schizophrenia are possibly caused by disturbances in low-level vision.
source: and reading disabilities (Revheim et al., 2006) possibly caused by the disturbances in low-level vision (Revheim et al., 2006; Lovegrove et al., 1980a).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The results suggest a potential link between fine-scale eye movements and visual deficits in dyslexia and schizophrenia, which has not yet been investigated and which may inspire novel therapeutic approaches.
source: Our results suggest a potential link between fine-scale eye movements and these visual deficits, which has not yet been investigated and which may inspire novel therapeutic approaches.
evidence: This is a speculation about clinical implications.

claim: Eye movements were recorded from five observers (all females, age range 21–31).
source: Eye movements were recorded from five observers (all females, age range 21–31).
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: Only subjects with normal, uncorrected vision took part in the study to optimize the precision of the recordings.
source: To optimize the precision of the recordings, only subjects with normal, uncorrected vision took part in the study.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: Only oculomotor traces collected around threshold levels of sensitivity and that contained no saccades, microsaccades or blinks were used in this study.
source: Only oculomotor traces collected around threshold levels of sensitivity and that contained no saccades, microsaccades or blinks were used in this study.
evidence: This describes the data selection criteria.

claim: Brownian motion, with D in the range 100–350, is known to be a good model for the normal retinal image motion when the head is not immobilized.
source: Brownian motion, with D in the range 100–350, is known to be a good model for the normal retinal image motion when the head is not immobilized (Aytekin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aytekin et al. 2014.
